newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican media magnate Azcarraga steps down.
newsitem.headline: Mexican media magnate Azcarraga steps down.

text.p: Mexican television tycoon Emilio Azcarraga Milmo resigned on Monday as head of Grupo Televisa SA, the largest media company in the Spanish-speaking world.
Known as "The Tiger" in part for his strongarm business tactics, the 66-year-old magnate stepped down for health reasons, the company said in a statement.

Azcarraga's television empire is widely believed to have helped to keep Mexico's ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) in control of the country's airwaves, and presidential seat, for decades.

One of Latin America's richest men, Azcarraga Milmo had taken a leave of absence from Televisa in early February to receive medical care in Los Angeles, prompting speculation that he might quit the post he had held since 1972.

Televisa tapped Azcarraga's son, Emilio Azcarraga Jean, as president and chief executive officer, the company said late on Monday. Azcarraga Jean is believed to be 28 years old, according to industry sources.

But with the apparent aim of limiting the younger Azcarraga's role, the company's board of directors also appointed former finance director Guillermo Canedo White as chairman and chief corporate officer, with responsibility for strategic planning, finance and corporate development.

"Truth be told, we are a bit tired ... the company needs young and aggressive blood," a haggard-looking Azcarraga Milmo said during a rare television interview broadcast on Televisa's "24 Horas" news programme.
Azcarraga Milmo added in a Televisa statement that his son and Canedo White had been sharing the responsibilities of Televisa's day-to-day duties "for some time now."

Televisa remained tight-lipped on Monday about what was wrong with the billionaire. Company officials had said he was having tests done on his heart, but would neither confirm nor deny rumours he had suffered a heart attack.

Televisa, which on Monday reported 1996 revenues of 11.5 billion pesos ($1.44 billion), sells its trademark Latin soap operas as far afield as China and Russia and is one of the world's biggest producers of programming in any language. It also runs a satellite TV project with Rupert Murdoch's News Corp. and U.S. cable giant TCI Communications.

Worry about the future of the firm without Azcarraga Milmo hurt the company's share price in recent weeks. Televisa's ADRs on Wall Street fell from a high of $34-5/8 in early January to $24 at the close of trade on Monday.

Flanked by his son and Canedo White, Azcarraga Milmo said he would remain in the honorary role of founding chairman at Televisa and work on projects related to satellite television, though not necessarily with Televisa.

Televisa said late on Monday it also named Miguel Aleman Velasco, head of satellite television projects, as vice chairman and Jaime Davila, head of the U.S.-based Univision network, as chief operating officer.

Azcarraga took over Televisa from his father, Emilio Azcarraga Vidaurrieta, and quickly consolidated its near-monopoly control over the Mexican airwaves, using a close relationship with the government to ensure scarce competition.

Stories of Azcarraga are part of Mexico's popular lore. During a fund-raiser for the PRI in 1993, he reportedly offered to pay $50 million from his own pocket to bankroll the government's re-election bid.
